facts.claim: "The Story" was written by Phil Hanseroth, not by Brandi Carlile. It is the title track of her 2007 second album.
T Bone Burnett produced the album. It was recorded over eleven days on two-inch audio tape at The Warehouse Studios in Vancouver, British Columbia.
The track was recorded in Vancouver with Tim Hanseroth on guitar, Phil Hanseroth on bass and Matt Chamberlain on drums.
The song was recorded "live to tape". All the performers played and sang at the same time instead of tracking their parts separately.

Burnett asked Carlile to sing the song without her acoustic guitar, because he thought the instrument was distracting her. She disagreed but put it down, and the take she recorded that way made the album.
Phil Hanseroth wrote the song before he and his twin brother Tim began working with Carlile. They have been her performing and writing partners since 2004.
Phil Hanseroth married Carlile's sister Tiffany.
In a 2013 Songfacts interview, Carlile said songs are "malleable". A love song can easily be heard as a song about someone's parents.
The song was featured in Grey's Anatomy on April 12, 2007, and appears on the Grey's Anatomy Soundtrack album 3.
Dolly Parton recorded the title track for Carlile's 2017 album Cover Stories, a track-by-track covers reimagining of The Story.

research.lineage: A folk-rock and Americana ballad from the Seattle-based Carlile and the Hanseroth twins, produced by T Bone Burnett, who is known for roots-music production.

draft:
The face does the talking first. **The Story** opens on "lines across my face," creases offered as a record of everything survived, and the first verse sounds almost proud of them. Then comes the turn: "But these stories don't mean anything / When you've got no one to tell them to." The pride doesn't go away. It turns out it was waiting on someone the whole time. By the song's own boasting, there were mountaintops climbed and an ocean swum, and the payoff for all of it is a single listener.

Phil Hanseroth wrote the song before he and his twin brother Tim began working with Brandi Carlile. So Carlile is singing another person's confession, and the fit is close enough that it's easy to forget. The third verse is where the confession gets honest. "It's hiding the words that don't come out," Carlile sings of a smile, and the friends who call the narrator blessed have no idea the head is a mess. Only the "you" knows. The devotion here is less pure romance than relief at being seen by one person while performing fine for everyone else. The swagger of breaking every rule sits right beside that admission, and the song never decides which is the truer picture.

Carlile has said songs are "malleable," that a love song can just as easily be heard as one about someone's parents. This one bears that out. Nothing in the lyric pins down what kind of love it is. It only says the love held up when the narrator was flat broke.

T Bone Burnett produced the album in eleven days at The Warehouse Studios in Vancouver. This song was cut live to tape, with everyone playing and singing at once: Tim Hanseroth on guitar, Phil on bass, Matt Chamberlain on drums. Burnett asked Carlile to put down the acoustic guitar to sing, thinking it was a distraction. Carlile disagreed, set it down anyway, and that take made the record. You can hear what it freed up. An arpeggiated acoustic figure and a root-note bass line give way to a driving rock beat with a strong snare backbeat. The voice rides over it clear and full, with a slight rasp, powerful and direct. Harmonies join in unison and thicken the lead. The sound is clean and polished but keeps a natural room around it. Burnett's roots-music ear is pointed at folk-rock that wants to be loud.

It's an Americana ballad that builds like a rock song. That suits a lyric about a mess hidden behind a smile, because the arrangement keeps adding weight until the composure sounds like effort.

What sticks is the moment pride gives way to need, when a lifetime of stories turns out to be worth nothing without the one person you'd tell them to.
